learningObjectives.title: Rate of reaction and collision theory

questions.q: How is the rate of a chemical reaction best defined?
options: The total mass of product made in a reaction
The change in amount of reactant used or product formed per unit time
The temperature reached at the end of a reaction
The concentration of the acid used in a reaction
questions.explain: Rate measures how quickly reactants are used up or products are formed over time.

questions.q: Why does increasing the temperature increase the rate of a reaction?
options: Particles gain mass and collide harder
Particles move faster, so they collide more frequently and more collisions have the activation energy
The activation energy of the reaction is lowered
Particles stop colliding but react more easily
questions.explain: Higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, increasing both collision frequency and the proportion of successful collisions.

questions.q: According to collision theory, a reaction only occurs when colliding particles have which of the following?
options: A minimum amount of energy called the activation energy, and the correct orientation
Equal masses and equal speeds
A catalyst attached to each particle
The same electrical charge
questions.explain: Particles must collide with at least the activation energy and in the right orientation for a reaction to happen.

questions.q: Why does increasing the concentration of a reactant in solution increase the rate of reaction?
options: The particles gain more energy
There are more reactant particles in a given volume, so collisions are more frequent
The activation energy is reduced
The particles become larger and easier to hit
questions.explain: A higher concentration packs more particles into the same volume, increasing the frequency of collisions.

questions.q: Breaking a solid reactant into smaller pieces increases the rate of reaction because it does what?
options: Increases the surface area exposed, so more collisions can occur
Increases the temperature of the reactants
Lowers the activation energy of the reaction
Reduces the number of particles present
questions.explain: Smaller pieces have a larger surface area to volume ratio, exposing more particles to collisions.

questions.q: Which of these is a suitable method for measuring the rate of a reaction that produces a gas?
options: Measuring the volume of gas collected over time
Measuring the colour of the solid catalyst
Weighing the reaction beaker before it is used
Measuring the room temperature over time
questions.explain: Collecting the gas produced (or measuring mass loss) over time allows the rate to be calculated.

questions.q: A student reacts magnesium ribbon with excess hydrochloric acid. They repeat the experiment using the same mass of magnesium powder instead. Compared with the ribbon, the powder will react how?
options: Faster, because the powder has a larger surface area
Slower, because the powder has less mass
At the same rate, because the mass is unchanged
Slower, because powder has a lower activation energy
questions.explain: Powder exposes more surface area than ribbon, increasing collision frequency and rate.

questions.q: What is a catalyst?
options: A substance that increases the rate of a reaction without being used up
A substance that is always used up in a reaction
A substance that raises the activation energy of a reaction
A substance that only works by increasing temperature
questions.explain: A catalyst speeds up a reaction but is not consumed, so it can be used again.

questions.q: What is the mass of a catalyst at the end of a reaction compared with the start?
options: It is unchanged, because the catalyst is not used up
It is greater, because the catalyst gains product
It is smaller, because the catalyst is consumed
It becomes zero, because the catalyst evaporates
questions.explain: Because a catalyst is not consumed, its mass is the same at the end as at the start.

questions.q: How does a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?
options: It provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy
It increases the activation energy so more collisions succeed
It raises the temperature of the reactants
It increases the concentration of the reactants
questions.explain: A catalyst offers a route with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

questions.q: What name is given to the biological catalysts found in living organisms?
options: Enzymes
Electrolytes
Isotopes
Polymers
questions.explain: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, speeding up reactions in living things.

questions.q: A student wants to speed up a reaction between an acid and a solid, but must keep the temperature and concentration the same. Which method should they use?
options: Add a suitable catalyst
Cool the mixture down
Use a smaller mass of solid
Dilute the acid with water
questions.explain: Adding a catalyst increases the rate without changing temperature or concentration.

questions.q: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings in an exothermic reaction?
options: It increases, because energy is transferred to the surroundings
It decreases, because energy is taken in from the surroundings
It stays exactly the same throughout
It first falls and then rises to the start value
questions.explain: Exothermic reactions release energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises.

questions.q: What happens to the temperature of the surroundings in an endothermic reaction?
options: It decreases, because energy is taken in from the surroundings
It increases, because energy is released to the surroundings
It stays the same because no energy is transferred
It rises above the boiling point of water
questions.explain: Endothermic reactions absorb energy from the surroundings, so the temperature falls.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of an exothermic reaction?
options: Combustion of a fuel
Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate
The reaction of citric acid with sodium hydrogencarbonate
Photosynthesis in plants
questions.explain: Combustion (like neutralisation and many oxidation reactions) releases energy, making it exothermic.

questions.q: In terms of energy, which statement about chemical bonds is correct?
options: Breaking bonds is endothermic and making bonds is exothermic
Breaking bonds is exothermic and making bonds is endothermic
Both breaking and making bonds release energy
Both breaking and making bonds absorb energy
questions.explain: Energy is needed to break bonds (endothermic) and energy is released when bonds form (exothermic).

questions.q: On a reaction profile for an exothermic reaction, how do the energy levels of the products compare with the reactants?
options: The products are at a lower energy level than the reactants
The products are at a higher energy level than the reactants
The products and reactants are at the same energy level
The products have no measurable energy
questions.explain: In an exothermic reaction the products store less energy than the reactants, and the difference is released.

questions.q: In a reaction, breaking the bonds in the reactants takes in 679 kJ and forming the bonds in the products releases 864 kJ. What is the overall energy change?
options: -185 kJ (exothermic)
+185 kJ (endothermic)
-1543 kJ (exothermic)
+1543 kJ (endothermic)
questions.explain: Energy change = energy in to break bonds - energy out to make bonds = 679 - 864 = -185 kJ, so it is exothermic.

questions.q: How is the overall energy change of a reaction calculated from bond energies?
options: Energy to break bonds in reactants minus energy released making bonds in products
Energy released making bonds in products minus energy to break bonds in reactants
Energy to break bonds added to energy to make bonds
Energy to make bonds multiplied by energy to break bonds
questions.explain: Overall energy change = total energy absorbed breaking bonds - total energy released forming bonds.

questions.q: When citric acid is added to sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, the temperature falls from 20 degrees C to 15 degrees C. What does this show about the reaction?
options: It is endothermic, because energy is taken in from the surroundings
It is exothermic, because energy is released to the surroundings
It is neither exothermic nor endothermic
No reaction has taken place
questions.explain: A fall in temperature shows energy is absorbed from the surroundings, so the reaction is endothermic.
